## Overview

The Turu, also called Arimi and Wanyaturu, are an ethnic and linguistic group based in the Singida Region of north-central Tanzania. Their original endonym is Arimi, meaning “farmers,” while Wanyaturu reflects contact with Swahili. In 1993, their population was estimated at 556,000, and the current population is stated to be over 1,000,000. The Turu speak Kinyaturu, a Bantu language also known as Turu, Nyaturu, Rimi Kirimi, Limi, and Remi. The group comprises the Airwana, Vahi, and Anyiŋanyi tribes, whose dialects remain mutually understandable despite differences. Their documented cultural life includes lineage-based social organization, cattle-centered economic activity, agricultural foodways, and ritual prayers addressed to God.

## Music & performance

The sources describe a traditional Turu hymn and ritual prayer called *Ukuta Yuva* in Kinyaturu, meaning “To praise the Sun.” It praises God and asks for blessings, while the *Yuva*, or Sun, symbolizes God. The prayer also pays homage to Mweri, the Moon, and Gimea, the Pleiades. During the prayer ritual, two elderly men sit facing each other; one recites the prayer slowly, while the other listens and bows. The listener repeatedly says “eheé eheé,” meaning “yes yes,” and “trute,” meaning “very true, Sir,” until the recitation ends.

## Festivals & rituals

They describe ritual prayers held on special occasions such as betrothal rituals. Turu people address their prayer to God during spiritual and emotional rituals, including the recitation of *Ukuta Yuva*. This prayer praises the power and goodness of the Sun and asks for divine blessings. The sources also describe a social organization based on lineage or ancestry. A village is described as a single level 2 lineage; several level 2 lineages form a clan, and several level 3 lineages form a subtribe. Chiefdoms are usually determined by patrilineal lineage and territory. The chief is described as the “eldest son of the senior wife of the clan’s founder,” although family elders of the royal sub-clan may elect a chief in cases of dissatisfaction or death. The chief and elders are described as preservers of the law, while elders teach young people their rights and obligations. Bride-wealth negotiations are conducted by representatives of the bride and groom and are paid over several years through cattle.

## Foodways

Turu economic activity is centered on acquiring cattle, with grain production providing the surplus used to purchase them at market. The main crops are *uwele*, maize, and *mtama*; cassava and sweet potatoes are also grown in the plateaus. Sunflowers and onions are among the commercial crops cultivated in recent years, although their commercial success is described as limited because of poor farming methods and unreliable weather. More than 70% of Nyaturu households are described as having ranch-like farming areas with cattle, goats, sheep, and chicken. Vahi people are also described as producers of honey and tobacco.

Food is described as a form of sociality that constitutes and mediates human interactions and social hierarchy. One staple food is *ugali*, a stiff porridge made from water, maize, millet, and sorghum flour. It is served with *mboga*, dried fish, meat, or greens. A popular Turu *mboga* is *Mlenda*, made from leafy greens, tomatoes, okra, salt, milk, and peanuts to form a green sauce.

## Oral tradition & literature

They do document the oral recitation of the prayer *Ukuta Yuva*, during which one elderly man recites slowly and another responds continuously with “eheé eheé” and “trute.”

## Language & religion

Kinyaturu is a Bantu language spoken by the Wanyaturu, also known as Arimi, in the Singida region of Tanzania. It is also called Turu, Nyaturu, Rimi Kirimi, Limi, and Remi. The language has dialects associated with the three Turu tribes: Girwana of the Airwana, Giahi of the Vahi, and Ginyamunyinganyi of the Anyiŋanyi. The sources state that the primary religion practiced among the Turu is Christianity. They also describe the Sun as highly important in Turu society and identify the Sun, Moon, and Pleiades in the prayer tradition.
